description:
LUNARIS: Lunar Mission Intelligence System

LUNARIS is a proposed interactive lunar mission planning platform designed to help researchers, engineers, and space enthusiasts evaluate potential Moon landing sites using NASA's scientific data.

The system aims to analyze solar illumination, Earth visibility, and communication opportunities across different lunar locations and mission dates. Through interactive visualizations and computational analysis, users will be able to compare landing sites, identify potential operational constraints, and understand the factors influencing mission planning.

Our objective is to transform complex astronomical data into an accessible, scientifically grounded decision-support tool, making lunar exploration planning more intuitive, transparent, and efficient.
summary: Lunaris answers "where should we land, and when?" for the Moon's south pole. A mission planner, teacher or curious visitor picks the landing dates and what matters most: sunlight, Earth in view for radio contact, short nights and gentle ground. Lunaris checks 18,073 points against each point's real terrain skyline, hour by hour, using NASA LOLA terrain and NASA/JPL SPICE positions of the Sun and Earth, and returns the best five sites in about half a second. For each site it shows the Sun and Earth moving against the real skyline, how sure the pick is (does it stay first if the arrival slips a few days or NASA's terrain height error is applied?), what breaks if the launch slips by weeks, and which nearby site still works. Visitors can stand on the site in 3D or VR and follow the journey from Earth orbit to touchdown. Every number is traceable to NASA data, and our sunlight map matches NASA's published polar illumination map (correlation 0.971, mean difference 1.6 points).
details:
What it does
Lunaris answers the question every south-pole Moon mission faces: where should we land, and when? You pick your landing dates and what matters most: sunlight for power, Earth in view for direct radio contact, short nights, gentle slopes. Lunaris ranks 18,073 points around the south pole and shows the best five sites in about half a second, each explained in plain English.

How it works

  1. Terrain: NASA's LOLA 240 m south-polar elevation map, with NASA's own per-pixel height-error map.
  2. Real skylines: for every point, our engine traces the terrain horizon in every direction, out to 500 km over the curved Moon.
  3. Sun and Earth: NASA/JPL SPICE positions for every hour from Nov 2026 to Dec 2028, in the same Moon frame as LOLA.
    • Our sunlight map next to NASA's, with zoom.
    • Stand on the site in 3D or VR and watch the Sun move along the real skyline.
    • Follow the journey from Earth orbit to touchdown.

Checks

  • Our long-term sunlight map matches NASA's published polar illumination map: correlation 0.971, mean difference 1.6 points.
  • SPICE positions agree with JPL Horizons to about 2 m.
  • Two independent implementations of the horizon engine and of the scoring agree.
  • Known bright places (Shackleton ridge, the connecting ridge, Malapert peak) land in our top few percent.

Benefits and impact
A planning check that takes experts hours per scenario becomes seconds, so teams can re-plan quickly when hardware or launch delays move the dates. It discovers sites instead of only checking ones you already know. It's free, runs in any browser with no sign-in, and works on phones, so students and teachers can explore real lunar planning data too.

Tools

  • Rust (horizon engine).
  • Python: NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, spiceypy.
  • TypeScript, Vite, three.js, WebXR, HTML canvas.
  • Hosted on Vercel.
  • AI coding assistants (Claude, Codex, Gemini) helped write and review code under our direction. The app itself contains no AI: every number comes from the engine and NASA data.

Creativity
Instead of a static map, Lunaris lets you see the answer: stand on the site, watch the Sun skim the real skyline, and see the exact moment it slips behind a ridge. Every value is labelled MEASURED, COMPUTED or SIMULATED, so you always know what is real data and what is illustration.

Factors we considered
Accuracy over looks (curved-Moon horizons, true Sun and Earth disk positions), honest limits (visibility is geometry, not watts or a guaranteed radio link; terrain resolution is 240 m), uncertainty from NASA's own error maps, plain English for non-experts, and speed on ordinary laptops and phones.

Team
We were a team of three working against the 36-hour clock. Splitting a project this large across three people was hard. The data processing, the engine and the 3D interface all depended on each other, so one person's change could break another's part. We kept it working by agreeing on fixed data formats early, testing every change against NASA's published maps, and cutting features that weren't reliable before the deadline.

Code: https://github.com/nearlyindifferent/lunaris
Live app: https://lunaris-demo.vercel.app
